newsitem.title: USA: Upper Midwest digs out from snowstorm.
newsitem.headline: Upper Midwest digs out from snowstorm.

text.p: Residents of the upper Midwest hauled away gigantic snowdrifts Monday using heavy construction equipment after a weekend blizzard closed roads and stranded travelers.
At least four fatalities were blamed on the fierce winter storm, including three people who died in a highway accident in South Dakota and a Minnesota man who fell off his roof while clearing snow.
Wisconsin residents used front-end loaders to tackle the huge drifts and North Dakota road crews called for a snowblower to tackle a huge mound of snow that cut off normally busy Interstate 29.
In Ashland, along the shore of Lake Superior in Wisconsin's "snow belt", cross-country skiiers were enjoying deep snow blown by strong winds into 20-foot snowbanks.

"All of the streets are opened, it's just that some of them are much narrower than they should be," Dawn Berglund of Ashland's Chamber of Commerce said. "It's bright and sunny, we have beautiful snow. I saw cross-country skiiers on Main Street."

The winter sport of snowmobiling was not as kind to Brad Lidtke, 30, who was caught outside overnight in the middle of the storm on Lake Winnibigoshish in northern Minnesota when his snowmobile broke down. He was rescued after 15 hours in sub-freezing temperatures and suffered frostbite on at least one foot, a spokeswoman at North Country Regional Hospital in Bemidji, Minnesota, said.
The roof of a Fargo, North Dakota, furniture store collapsed under the weight of two feet of snow and ice, causing an estimated $2 million in damage but no injuries, state officials said.

Many highways across the region were reopening Monday, although motels and rest stops along Interstate 29 in eastern North Dakota were still crowded with drivers stranded since Saturday. Officials were concerned that even as snowdrifts were removed a layer of ice would make for hazardous driving.
"Part of the problem is they had rain Friday that then turned into snow. So there's a slippery road underneath," Kathleen Donahue of North Dakota's emergency management agency said.

The deepest snow fell across the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin and the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, where it was still snowing heavily Monday morning. In Duluth, Minnesota, where 18 inches (46 cm) of snow fell, many residents bought their groceries early Saturday, then stayed home to wait out the storm.
"I don't mean to sound like we're a bunch of stoic people but this wasn't too bad," the city's communications manager Steve Greenfield said. Temperatures dipped below zero Monday.

The National Weather Service predicted another storm would sweep through the region Wednesday, bringing up to eight inches of snow and bitter cold. Several cities in the upper Midwest, including Duluth, had already exceeded their normal allotment of snow for an entire winter season.
"It's usually the end of March before we see the ground again," the Weather Service's John Margraf in Minneapolis said.
